passage: Understanding India's drainage system requires looking beyond just the main river channels. A drainage basin is defined as the entire area of land drained by a single river system, including all its tributaries and smaller streams. In India, rivers follow diverse paths based on the slope of the land. While many flow eastwards into the Bay of Bengal, others like the Narmada and Tapi flow westwards into the Arabian Sea, proving that not all rivers move from north to south. The source of water also varies significantly. Himalayan rivers are perennial, meaning they flow throughout the year, primarily because they are fed by both melting glaciers and seasonal rainfall. In contrast, many peninsular rivers are seasonal, relying solely on rain. Finally, we must recognize that river pollution is a complex issue. While industrial waste is a major contributor, the degradation of water quality is also significantly worsened by urban sewage discharge, agricultural runoff, and the dumping of solid waste by local communities. Protecting our rivers requires addressing these multiple sources of contamination rather than blaming a single cause.

items.evidence: A drainage basin is defined as the entire area of land drained by a single river system, including all its tributaries and smaller streams.
items.q: A small stream feeds a tributary of the Godavari. Which basin does the stream's land belong to?
options: The Godavari basin, along with its tributaries
No basin, since a basin is the channel
No basin, since a wall divides the waters
Its own basin, since each stream has one
items.explain: A drainage basin is all the land drained by one river system, including tributaries and small streams.

wrong.why: thinks a basin is only the river channel
thinks a water divide is a built wall
thinks every small stream forms a separate basin

items.evidence: While many flow eastwards into the Bay of Bengal, others like the Narmada and Tapi flow westwards into the Arabian Sea, proving that not all rivers move from north to south.
items.q: A leaf floats down the Narmada until it reaches the sea. Where does it end up?
options: The Arabian Sea, by flowing west
The Bay of Bengal, by flowing east
The Indian Ocean, by flowing south
The Arabian Sea, by flowing south
items.explain: The Narmada flows westwards into the Arabian Sea, unlike most rivers that flow east.

wrong.why: thinks the Narmada flows east like most peninsular rivers
thinks all Indian rivers flow north to south
knows the sea but keeps the north-to-south idea

items.evidence: Himalayan rivers are perennial, meaning they flow throughout the year, primarily because they are fed by both melting glaciers and seasonal rainfall.
items.q: Why do Himalayan rivers keep flowing even in the dry months?
options: Melting glaciers feed them as well as rain
Heavy rainfall alone keeps them full
Their steep slope keeps the water moving
Seasonal rivers join them in dry months
items.explain: Himalayan rivers get water from melting glaciers and rain, so they flow all year.

wrong.why: thinks rainfall alone makes them perennial
picks the slope detail from a nearby sentence
misreads seasonal rivers as a water source

items.evidence: While industrial waste is a major contributor, the degradation of water quality is also significantly worsened by urban sewage discharge, agricultural runoff, and the dumping of solid waste by local communities.
items.q: A river near a town has no factories, yet its water is dirty. How can this be?
options: Sewage, farm runoff and garbage also pollute it
Factory waste must be secretly reaching it
Glacier melt brings dirt from the mountains
Seasonal rain alone makes the water dirty
items.explain: Besides factory waste, city sewage, farm runoff and dumped garbage also pollute rivers.

wrong.why: thinks only industrial waste pollutes rivers
picks the glacier detail from an earlier sentence
blames one single cause instead of many
